title: The Symposium
author: Plato
edition_analyzed: Standard academic translation (e.g., Benjamin Jowett, Penguin Classics, or Oxford World’s Classics edition)
target_audience: Scholars and students of philosophy and classics
Readers interested in ancient Greek literature and culture
Individuals exploring the origins of Western thought
Those interested in love, relationships, and ethics
core_themes: The nature and meaning of love (Eros)
Philosophical discourse and the pursuit of truth
The ascent from physical attraction to spiritual and intellectual love (the Ladder of Love)
The role of love in creativity and knowledge
primary_purpose: To explore and examine the nature of love through a series of speeches given by various prominent Athenians (and Socrates), each presenting their distinct perspective, ultimately leading to Plato’s philosophical insights on love’s role in personal growth and the apprehension of higher truths.

structure_format.narrative_style: Dialogic; narrated as a recollection within a frame narrative
structure_format.organization: A sequence of speeches at a banquet, with each speaker providing a different view on love
features: Speeches by historical and literary figures (Phaedrus, Pausanias, Eryximachus, Aristophanes, Agathon, Socrates, Alcibiades)

key_concepts_lessons: Love (Eros) takes many forms, ranging from physical attraction to a quest for the eternal and the divine.
True love inspires individuals to pursue wisdom and beauty beyond the physical realm.
The ‘Ladder of Love’ metaphor shows how love can elevate the soul from base desire to intellectual and spiritual fulfillment.
Love acts as a motivator for both creativity and virtue.
The search for truth and the good life is inherently tied to the experience of love.
style_tone: Mix of playful banter and profound philosophizing
notable_features: Dramatic setting at a drinking party (symposium) in Athens
Mix of historical, fictional, and mythological discourse
Includes Aristophanes’ famous myth of the original humans split in half
Socrates presents Diotima’s Ladder of Love, a foundational concept in Western philosophy
Alcibiades’ comedic and poignant speech on Socrates adds a personal, human touch
cultural_historical_context: Written in classical Athens, The Symposium reflects the intellectual ferment of the 4th century BCE, including the role of the symposium as a social and intellectual institution and diverse Greek attitudes toward love, virtue, and knowledge. It has influenced centuries of philosophical, literary, and artistic reflection on love.
reception_impact: Canonized as one of the foundational works of Western philosophy and literature
Instrumental in shaping Western notions of love, beauty, and philosophical method
Studied and cited by thinkers from antiquity to the present day (including Christian, Renaissance, and modern philosophers)
Particularly influential in discussions of Platonic love and the relationship between desire and the pursuit of truth
comparable_titles: On Love by Stendhal (as a later literary/philosophical treatment of love)
